text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London closed sharply lower in a correction to recent sharp gains and following renewed African and Far Eastern origin selling. January lost $60 to close at $1,537 per tonne, while March gave up $38 to close at $1,532 per tonne. The market will watch next week's talks in Indonesia among robusta producers on export quota allocations. The ACPC recently decided that robusta growers would have to trim exports by 1 million bags in the first half of 1997. In New York arabica futures closed sharply lower in a technical correction to the market's recent sharp run-up and an unconfirmed report about the size of the Brazilian 1997/98 crop. BRAZIL - A preliminary forecast of Brazil's 1997/98 (May/April) coffee crop by former USDA Attache Leon Yalouz suggested the 1997/98 coffee crop will be more than 27 million bags which differs sharply from preliminary estimates by the Brazilian government, which have pegged the crop at between 18 and 20 million bags compared with an estimated 25 million bags a year earlier. Yalouz based his preliminary forecast on field trips made in September 1996. However, he is presently engaged in field studies to prepare a revised estimate.

GUATEMALA - Coffee production in Guatemala in 1996/97 (October/September) will be lower than expected and significantly down on last year. According to the National Coffee Association (Anacafe) the total in 1996/97 will not exceed 3.0 million bags, down from 3.6 million bags produced in 1995/96 and 3.8 million bags produced in 1994/95. Anacafe attributed the fall to strong rains in August and September.

COLOMBIA - Colombia will announce cuts in coffee exports next week under the terms of a beefed up retention plan agreed on January 23 by members of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC), National Coffee Growers Federation chief Jorge Cardenas said. He declined to say by how much Colombia was likely to cut its exports but under the ACPC deal arabica producing nations will hold back an additional 300,000 bags in the first half of 1997.

ITALY - Italy imported 539,032 bags of coffee in July 1996, 9.9 per cent more than was imported the same month the previous year. That brought total imports since the beginning of 1996 up to 3.479 million bags, 5 per cent more than was imported the same year-ago period. Total imports in calendar year 1995 dropped by 1.6 per cent to 5.387 million bags. Major suppliers of green coffee in January/July 1996 were Cameroon (252,700 vs 220,300 bags), Ivory Coast (279,100 vs 289,700 bags), Zaire (310,500 vs 443,600 bags), Brazil (742,300 vs 918,500 bags), Colombia (245,700 vs 182,600 bags) and India (285,000 vs 235,700 bags).
